title: The fast of Dawud
hook: a day on, a day off, the most beloved fast (Bukhari)
carry: a day on, a day off

segments.voice: Yesterday, the white days, and your line: the full-moon days. Did you catch the moon, and how round was it? Day one thousand one hundred thirteen.

What do you do with someone who wants to do too much good? Abdullah ibn Amr was a companion with a big plan. Word reached the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ that Abdullah had vowed to fast every single day and stand in prayer every single night, for as long as he lived. The Prophet came to him and asked if it was true. It was. What came next wasn't praise, and it wasn't a scolding either. It was a negotiation, step by step, that ended at a fast with a name. Today, the fast of Dawud.
screen: `TOO MUCH GOOD?` → `EVERY DAY, EVERY NIGHT.` → `A NEGOTIATION.`

segments.voice: First, the bargaining. The account is in Sahih al-Bukhari. The Prophet tells Abdullah: you can't keep that up. Fast and break your fast, sleep and stand in prayer. Fast three days a month. Abdullah says he can do more. More is offered, and he asks for more again, until the Prophet says: then fast the fast of Dawud. Fast a day, and break a day. And when Abdullah asks for still more, the answer is that there is nothing better than that. Second, the reason. In the same report, the Prophet tells him that his body has a right over him, and his eyes, and his wife, and his guests. Worship isn't meant to swallow the rest of a life. Third, the name. Dawud is David, the prophet whom the Qur'an remembers for the psalms he was given. Another hadith in Bukhari says the most beloved fast to Allah is the fast of Dawud, who fasted one day and did not fast the next, and the most beloved prayer is his prayer, sleeping, rising, and sleeping again. A rhythm, not a marathon. Fourth, the ending. In the report, Abdullah lives long, and in old age he wishes he had taken the Prophet's easier offer. Another version in Bukhari says he kept to his word anyway. It's a striking thing for a collection to preserve: a companion admitting he asked for too much. Look back over this week and the same thread runs through it. The fast bends for the ill and the traveler. Missed days are made up. Some feed instead. The fast is a shield, not a weapon. Two days a week, three days a month. And today, at the far edge of what's encouraged, a day on and a day off, with rest built in.
screen: `ABDULLAH ASKS FOR MORE.` · `YOUR BODY HAS A RIGHT OVER YOU.` · `DAWUD'S RHYTHM: ON, THEN OFF.` · `AN OLD MAN KEEPS HIS WORD.`

segments.voice: The practice: read about it, and then let it sit. You've just heard the story. Now settle, and breathe in and out, slowly. Notice the rhythm: in, then out. Effort, then rest. One isn't better than the other; the breath needs both. Now think of one thing in your own life you've been doing every single day, without a break, and ask what a day off from it would look like. Don't decide anything. Just let the question breathe with you. The bell holds the time.
The fast of Dawud. Fasting one day and eating the next, named for the prophet David, and called in Bukhari the most beloved fast to Allah. Today's word.
Your line: a day on, a day off. Today, give one thing you push at daily a short rest, and see what comes back. Tomorrow: Arafah and Ashura. Day one thousand one hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Some Muslims keep the fast of Dawud, fasting every other day, and the story of Abdullah ibn Amr is told as a caution against taking on more than one can sustain.

notes: Bukhari 1976 and 1975 (Abdullah ibn Amr's bargaining; 'your body has a right over you', eyes, wife, guests): confirm numbers and that the guest and old-age regret details are in these versions (the regret also appears in Bukhari 5052).
Bukhari 1131 (most beloved fast and prayer are Dawud's): confirm number and the description of the night prayer (sleep half, pray a third, sleep a sixth), summarized here without numbers.
Qur'an 4:163 cited for Dawud given the Psalms (Zabur), paraphrased.
